questions.q: According to this lesson, where is RLAIF's advantage over human-labeled RLHF largest?
options: On tasks that depend heavily on individual subjective taste

When far more preference comparisons are needed than a human pipeline can produce in the available time or budget, especially for recurring labeling needs, and on principle-based tasks where a rubric applies consistently
Only when the model being trained is smaller than the judge model
RLAIF has no advantage over RLHF in any scenario
questions.explain: Scale, recurring labeling needs, and tasks where consistent rubric application matters more than nuance are where RLAIF's case is strongest.

questions.q: Why is a harm-avoidance task like Constitutional AI's harmlessness use case a particularly good fit for RLAIF?
options: Because harm-avoidance questions have no well-defined answer at all
Because 'does this response follow principle X' is a reasonably well-defined question an AI judge can apply consistently, unlike open-ended questions where human taste and context vary
Because harmlessness cannot be judged by any method other than RLAIF
Because harm-avoidance tasks require no judging criteria whatsoever
questions.explain: Principle-based questions with reasonably well-defined answers are a good match for consistent AI judging, unlike tasks like creativity or personalized helpfulness where taste genuinely varies.

questions.q: What did Google's RLAIF paper (Lee et al., 2023) actually report, and what is its scope?
options: That RLAIF outperforms RLHF on every possible task and domain
That AI-labeled preferences reached roughly the same human-rater-judged quality as human-labeled RLHF, specifically on a summarization task — a useful but narrow data point
That human labeling is always superior and RLAIF never matches it
That no comparison between RLAIF and RLHF has ever been published
questions.explain: The parity result is specific to summarization and one judge-prompt design; it doesn't establish that RLAIF matches RLHF universally.

questions.q: Why can an AI judge's consistency become a liability rather than an asset on subjective, taste-dependent tasks?
options: Consistency is always beneficial regardless of the task
An AI judge will confidently and uniformly apply its own biases across every comparison, rather than surfacing the genuine diversity of human opinion that exists on tasks like creative writing style
AI judges cannot produce consistent outputs under any circumstances
Subjective tasks have no preference variation among human raters either
questions.explain: On tasks where the 'right' answer genuinely depends on taste or context, applying one judge's criteria uniformly erases real diversity of human opinion rather than capturing it.

questions.q: Why does human-labeled data still matter even when primarily using an AI judge for RLAIF, according to this lesson?
options: It doesn't — once an AI judge is set up, human-labeled data serves no further purpose
Human-labeled comparisons are needed to validate whether the AI judge's preferences actually track real quality or just its own blind spots, mirroring the independent-correlation check from lesson 40
Human-labeled data is only needed to train the base pretrained model, unrelated to RLAIF
Human-labeled data is required solely to set the KL penalty coefficient
questions.explain: Without some human-labeled comparisons to check against, there's no way to know if the AI judge's preferences reflect true quality rather than its own systematic blind spots.
